title: The Built Environment and Spatial Form
authors: Denise L. Lawrence and Setha M. Low, 1990
review_question: To define major research areas, critically evaluate contributions, and suggest future directions for understanding human interactions with the built environment in anthropology.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Includes built forms (building types, defined/bounded spaces, landmarks, specific building elements, spatial subdivisions, site plans). Excludes natural environment/landscape, large-scale settlement patterns, archaeoastronomy, material culture/traditional arts, and applied anthropology/housing issues in developing countries.

findings.consequent: Accommodation of collective endeavors of coresident families
findings.quote: Lewis Henry Morgan observed that aboriginal house forms were designed to accommodate the collective endeavors of several coresident families.

findings.consequent: Integration into social life, product of classificatory processes, model for reproducing social forms
findings.quote: Durkheim (87) and Durkheim & Mauss (88) similarly saw the built environment as an integral part of social life.

findings.consequent: Adaptation to annual climatic changes, accommodation of collective ritual intensification
findings.quote: Mauss described the seasonal variations in house form as essential to the adaptation of Eskimo society to annual climatic changes.

findings.consequent: Built forms
findings.quote: According to Rapoport, built forms are primarily influenced by sociocultural factors modified by architectural responses both to climatic conditions and to limitations of materials and methods.

findings.consequent: Architectural forms
findings.quote: Architects continue to be fascinated with finding and describing parallels between symbolic structures and architectural forms.

findings.consequent: Variability and distribution of built forms
findings.quote: Explanation of the variability and distribution of built forms has also been the continuing concern of some geographers, folklorists, and historians of vernacular architecture, some of whom have critically applied the concept of diffusion by focusing on sociocultural interactions.

findings.consequent: Stimulus for altering dwelling spatial configuration
findings.quote: Variability, in the form of shifting sizes and relationships as people experience life-cycle changes, provides a potential and continuing stimulus for altering the spatial configuration of the dwelling.

findings.consequent: Coincidence with physical boundaries of the dwelling
findings.quote: Thus, these studies indicate that the social boundaries of household units do not necessarily coincide with the physical boundaries of the dwelling itself.

findings.consequent: Increased partitioning and monofunctional uses of spaces in built forms
findings.quote: Kent argues that increasing social complexity in the form of specialization and stratification is expressed in the increased partitioning and monofunctional uses of spaces in built forms.

findings.consequent: Population size or postmarital residence practices
findings.quote: Dwelling size may be an indicator of population size [with a proposed universal of 10 m²/person (262)] or of postmarital residence practices (73, 99).

findings.consequent: Sedentary societies, easier additions, longer occupation, larger groupings of independent households, nucleated settlements
findings.quote: Rectangular forms, which tend to be more permanent than round ones, have been found associated with sedentary societies (379), although nomadic societies may have round or rectangular forms.

findings.antecedent: Construction permanence (e.g., mud huts vs. permanent structures)
findings.consequent: Degree of fit between social organization and built form
findings.quote: David argues that the definition of fit is specific to each culture and must be discovered by the ethnographer (68).

findings.antecedent: Changes due to developmental cycle (in permanent construction)
findings.consequent: Lack of fit in dwelling
findings.quote: Where construction is more permanent, a lack of fit is repeatedly introduced into the dwelling by changes due to the developmental cycle (161, 178, 274).

findings.consequent: Expression of social organization changes in built form (e.g., larger houses for larger domestic groups)
findings.quote: Household wealth, however, determines whether changes in social organization find expression in built form (205).

findings.consequent: Utilitarian ends (mediating human-environment, accommodating behavior) and symbolic purposes (expressing status differences)
findings.quote: Built forms serve utilitarian ends, mediating human relations with the natural environment and accommodating behavioral requirements; they have symbolic purposes such as expressing status differences.

findings.antecedent: Society's sedentary nature and wealth accumulation
findings.consequent: Shift from temporary round structures (low construction, high maintenance) to permanent rectangular buildings (high construction, low maintenance)
findings.quote: As societies become more sedentary, and wealth accumulates, permanent rectangular buildings are built, reversing construction and maintenance cost relations.

findings.consequent: Constant rebuilding, adaptation to developmental cycle, and moving houses to reaffirm patrilocal residence/land claims
findings.quote: Because of the impermanence of housing materials in tropical climates, the people of Vanuatu must constantly rebuild their houses, adapting them to changes brought about by the developmental cycle of the household.

findings.consequent: Household choices in altering dwelling forms to conform to familial needs
findings.quote: Schwertdfeger concludes that larger socioeconomic forces beyond the domestic group condition the choices and abilities of households in altering dwelling forms to conform to familial needs.

findings.consequent: Specialization of domestic space by sex (e.g., privacy, separation)
findings.quote: The most extreme example of spatial segregation is found in Near Eastern Muslim societies observing purdah.

findings.consequent: Changes in dwelling form and behavior (e.g., traditional tent plans to specialized spaces)
findings.quote: Layne (227) examines Bedouins who become sedentary as a result of their increasing integration into the capitalist system.

findings.consequent: Corresponding change in social behavior
findings.quote: However, not every change in built form causes or is caused by a corresponding change in social behavior (49, 326).

findings.consequent: Symbolization of dimensions of political and social structure
findings.quote: The clearest exposition of this approach is Hilda Kuper's seminal argument that specific locations symbolize dimensions of Swazi political and social structure (210).

findings.consequent: Expression of institutionalized strategies for presenting the self as a member of a particular social group
findings.quote: The most developed thesis on housing and identity relations is Duncan's (83), who argues from studies in the United States and India that different domestic forms and their landscapes express institutionalized strategies for presenting the self as a member of a particular social group (81, 82).

findings.antecedent: Collectivistic images (closed social groups, segregated sexual division of labor)
findings.consequent: Houses seen as containers of women
findings.quote: Duncan further argues that collectivistic images are associated with closed social groups and a segregated sexual division of labor; these houses are seen as containers of women.

findings.antecedent: Individualism (open social groups, high mobility, less sexual segregation)
findings.consequent: Houses seen as status symbols
findings.quote: Individualism is characterized by open social groups, high mobility, and less sexual segregation; these houses are seen as status symbols (83).

findings.consequent: Patterned cultural behaviors, including built forms
findings.quote: Lévi-Strauss postulates the existence of (a) a structured collective unconscious capable of generating patterned cultural behaviors, including built forms; and (b) unconscious mental structures comprised of binary oppositions that represent universal characteristics of human thought (231).

findings.antecedent: Objectification of symbolic oppositions inside the house
findings.consequent: Inculcation of habitus (generative/structuring principle of collective strategies/social practices)
findings.quote: Bourdieu locates a principal mechanism for inculcating habitus in the objectification of symbolic oppositions found inside the house.

findings.consequent: Metaphor for universe organization, integration of body space and cosmic space through gender principles
findings.quote: In the Kabyle example, the home is a metaphor for the organization of the universe structured on gender principles; it is the setting in which body space and cosmic space are integrated through practice.

findings.consequent: Design and development of folk housing styles
findings.quote: His inferences from particular household architectural configurations lead him to conclude that formal geometries rather than environmental or behavioral needs guided design and development of folk housing styles.

findings.consequent: Expression and direction of social processes (sociability, controlling behavior in host-guest/insider-outsider relations)
findings.quote: Built forms not only express but direct and shape social processes concerned with sociability and controlling behavior in host-guest or insider-outsider relations.

findings.consequent: Language-like sign systems or codes (architectural semiotics)
findings.quote: A final area of research that can only be mentioned here is the field of architectural semiotics. Semiotic approaches liken the built environment to a language; the formal characteristics constitute sign systems or codes.

findings.consequent: Metaphorical expression of cosmology, myth, social structure, and cultural meaning systems
findings.quote: His monograph is an elaborate and detailed exegesis that links cosmology, myth, social structure, and village architecture through cultural meaning systems.

findings.consequent: Metaphor writ large, isomorphic with life, means for ordering experience
findings.quote: The built environment for the Batammaliban represents every facet of personal, social, and cultural life, and is isomorphic with life itself.

findings.consequent: Metaphoric progression of structural replication of political and domestic social structure
findings.quote: A similar but less complete example of the metaphoric power of architecture links architectural form to social structure (254); for the Cuna, traditional architecture expresses in metaphoric progression the structural replication of all Cuna political and domestic social structure arrayed in multiple, serial, and rank orders.

findings.antecedent: Territorial organization, village structure, house plan (Dogon)
findings.consequent: Anthropomorphic representation of seed, procreation, gestation, germination (cultural ideas)
findings.quote: He describes how territorial organization represents the form of the seed, a central symbol in Dogon mythology.

findings.consequent: Metaphorical correspondence with landscape, used to understand each other, transmitting memory, morality, emotion
findings.quote: Another group of anthropologists have developed a metaphorical correspondence between the human body and the landscape.

findings.consequent: Critical symbolic elements during ritual performances, providing setting/markers for collective transcendence/communitas
findings.quote: Both temporary and permanent features of the built environment act as critical symbolic elements during ritual performances by providing setting and markers for the participants' collective transcendence of ordinary reality and passage into communitas, a temporary collective state of total unity (363, 364).

findings.antecedent: Performative aspects of ritual and social drama
findings.consequent: Imbuing built environment elements with social and symbolic significance
findings.quote: A number of studies emphasize how performative aspects of ritual and social drama imbue elements of the built environment with social and symbolic significance, some becoming metaphors embodying complex meanings.

findings.antecedent: Space (e.g., plaza, market in Costa Rica)
findings.consequent: Experience of being-in-the-world, communication of basic cultural dynamics
findings.quote: In Richardson's perspective, space is the experience of being-in-the-world—that is, the existential or phenomenological reality of the place: its smell, feel, color, etc.

findings.consequent: Disguised representation of latent sexual thoughts
findings.quote: According to Freud (122), symbols are inherently sexual and are used for the disguised representation of latent thoughts.

findings.consequent: Fundamental symbol, protector of the self, link to primordial collective past (archetype)
findings.quote: The best known application of this perspective to the built environment is found in Cooper's (58) classic exploration of the house as a fundamental symbol, as well as protector, of the self.

findings.consequent: Models of sacred space, representing cosmological center (archetype)
findings.quote: Eliade argues that the built forms in nonliterate societies are models of sacred space, representing the cosmological center of the world, achieving unification through the central pole or axis mundi (98).

findings.consequent: Integral to psychological concept of the self (infant introjects environment)
findings.quote: In The Non-Human Environment, Harold Searles (346) offers a psychoanalytic theory of human development that includes the spatial environment as integral to the psychological concept of the self.

findings.consequent: Structuring space in relation to genital modes (boys: high structures/downfalls; girls: static interiors/enclosed spaces)
findings.quote: Erik Erikson, on the other hand, views symbols as expressions of interpsychic developmental processes. In Childhood and Society (101), he presents case histories of how children playing with blocks structure the space in relation to their genital modes.

findings.consequent: Conditioning of spatial perception (e.g., susceptibility to optical illusions)
findings.quote: The researchers argued that the perception of space stems from learning conditioned by different ecological and cultural environments.

findings.consequent: Modification of innate distancing mechanism (personal space) to regulate social contact
findings.quote: Hall postulates that humans may have an innate distancing mechanism, modified by culture, that helps to regulate contact in social situations.

findings.consequent: Communicative features (nonverbal communication)
findings.quote: Ultimately, the spatial dimension of behavior has communicative features: 'Space speaks' (150).

findings.consequent: Ability to survive high densities, development of elaborate rules/practices to reduce density-related stresses
findings.quote: People of certain cultures may even seek high-density settings. In doing so, they develop elaborate rules and practices that ostensibly reduce density-related stresses.

findings.consequent: Variation in expression, achievement through rules regulating interpersonal behavior rather than direct environmental manipulation
findings.quote: In a cross-cultural study, Altman (8) concludes that expression of a desire for privacy varies greatly. In fact, he finds privacy is achieved more often through rules regulating interpersonal behavior rather than by direct manipulation of the environment.

findings.antecedent: Territoriality expressed in the environment (hierarchy of recognized spaces, symbolic markers)
findings.consequent: Regulation of behavior, enhanced control
findings.quote: When territoriality is expressed in the environment through a hierarchy of recognized spaces or symbolic markers, behavior may be regulated and control enhanced (266).

findings.antecedent: Actors' presentations and representations of self (in spaces, situations, self)
findings.consequent: Convincing others of identity (dramaturgical performance)
findings.quote: Goffman identifies qualities of territoriality in spaces, situations, and in the self (138), and forcefully demonstrates how all three combine in actors' presentations and representations aimed at convincing others of who they are.

findings.consequent: Expressive ends, regulation of behavior through dialectical oppositions of identity/community and openness/closedness
findings.quote: A cross-cultural comparison of the home reveals how the linkage of psychological and physical features serves expressive ends and aids in the regulation of behavior through the dialectical oppositions of identity/community and openness/closedness (11).

findings.antecedent: Taking control of a particular place
findings.consequent: Actualization of self and identity ('appropriation of space')
findings.quote: An alternative concept, 'appropriation of space,' has also been used by some European researchers. This Marx-inspired term emphasizes the actualization of self and identity in the taking of control of a particular place (202).

findings.consequent: Description of built forms and exploration of their meanings
findings.quote: Linguistic categories are extensively used in some ethnographies to describe built forms and explore their meanings (234, 241, 337), and, of course, structuralist interpretations have consistently attended to language (267, 354).

findings.consequent: Massive destruction of neighborhoods/communities, social problems/pathologies of new town planning
findings.source: Studies of Urban Redevelopment and Resettlement
findings.quote: These studies were generated out of a concern for the massive destruction of neighborhoods and communities caused by urban renewal projects of the 1950s and 1960s, and by the social problems and pathologies of new town planning.

findings.consequent: Politically charged processes, often unrelated to user needs/desires
findings.source: Studies of Urban Redevelopment and Resettlement
findings.quote: All these studies show housing and planning to be politically charged processes and argue that squatter housing, urban renewal, urban redevelopment, and new town planning have little to do with the needs and desires of users or the actions of individual architects and planners.

findings.antecedent: Buildings and the entire built environment
findings.consequent: Social and cultural products, accommodating functions, governed by society's ideas/organization/resources/values
findings.quote: According to Anthony D. King, the major proponent of the social history of built forms, 'buildings, indeed, the entire built environment, are essentially social and cultural products.'

findings.consequent: Emergence of new buildings, obsolescence of others, maintenance/reinforcement of social forms
findings.quote: King (192) goes on to note that as society changes new buildings emerge and others become obsolete. Society produces buildings that maintain and/or reinforce its social forms.

findings.consequent: Contribution to power of some groups over others, object of social struggle
findings.quote: The contributors of this special issue, theoretically influenced by Marxist geographers, focus on how particular geographic arrangements support social relations of different modes of production and the historical process of spatial transformation.

findings.consequent: Creation of 'docile body', control of space through enclosure and organization of individuals
findings.quote: Foucault uses the model of Jeremy Bentham's 1787 plan for the panopticon to represent an architectural mechanism of control in its ideal form.

findings.consequent: Ensuring allocation of people in space, canalization of their circulation, maintenance of power relations
findings.quote: For him, architecture exists to 'insure a certain allocation of people in space, a canalization of their circulation' (118).

findings.consequent: Insights into modern world system development, definition of new spaces, creation of work, representation of changing social structures, maintenance of economic/social/political/cultural practices
findings.quote: According to King (196) the architecture of colonialism provides insights into the developmental processes of the modern world system.

findings.consequent: Laboratory for political effectiveness of new, large-scale planning concepts, links between modern political power, aesthetic theories, knowledge
findings.quote: Rabinow links the growth of modern forms of political power with the evolution of aesthetic theories and shows how the colonialists sought to use architecture and city planning to demonstrate the cultural superiority of the French...

findings.consequent: Regulation of urban space, rather than governmental power
findings.quote: In fact, in Nantes not the state but individual capitalists are responsible for planning space. Economy and society begin to set the guidelines for urban development; commercial flow, rather than governmental power, regulates the use of space thereafter.

findings.consequent: Creation of new society, maintenance of social hierarchy, representation of modern French norms
findings.quote: Lyautey's solution was to create a new society by finding French agents who could direct the modernization of the Moroccan nobility. The form of this program was to build villes nouvelles, modern French settlements, next to but separate from Morocco's existing cities.

findings.consequent: Reproduction of sociopolitical organization (ideological ends), social resistance/conflict in determining urban organization/form
findings.quote: Manuel Castells (52) argues that architecture and planning serve unacknowledged ideological ends in reproducing a structure of sociopolitical organization that itself lies at the root of urban problems. But Castells (53) adds the critical dimension of social resistance and conflict in determining urban organization and form.

findings.consequent: Production of spatial forms, expression of dominant class interests, resistance from exploited classes
findings.quote: Therefore spatial forms will be produced by human action, as are all other objects, and will express and perform the interests of the dominant class according to a given mode of production and to a specific mode of development.

findings.antecedent: Design and plan for implementation of Brasilia
findings.consequent: Unintended processes of social and urban planning, diverse resident reactions
findings.quote: Holston's (169) critique of the design and plan for implementation of Brasilia as a created symbol intended to transform Brazilian society and be an instrument for social change is the most recent example of a critical ethnography that explores the unintended processes of social and urban planning.

findings.consequent: Integral to occurrence of social behavior, not merely an environment
findings.quote: Anthony Gidden's (128–130) theory of structuration argues that space must be incorporated into social theory, not as an environment, but as integral to the occurrence of social behavior.

findings.consequent: Transformation of social system at the level of social action
findings.quote: In Gidden's model the individual elements of the interaction transform the social system at the level of social action as the individual behaviors and movements actually make-up the social world.

findings.consequent: Social reproduction (process based on performance of these activities)
findings.quote: For Giddens, social reproduction is a process based on the performance of everyday activities and behaviors.

findings.antecedent: Practice and social reproduction of rules/power relations, parallel emergence of socially produced 'spatial structure'
findings.consequent: Duration of social hierarchies
findings.quote: He argues that the duration of social hierarchies depended 'upon an uninterrupted dialectic between practice itself and the social reproduction of rules and power relations, and upon the parallel emergence of a socially produced 'spatial structure' (291:254).

findings.antecedent: Local practice, utilization of fields, individual daily/life paths, institutional projects
findings.consequent: Transformation of Swedish social structure
findings.quote: Changes in local practice, the utilization of fields, the dialectics of individual daily and life paths, and institutional projects are shown to have transformed Swedish social structure (293).

findings.consequent: Hegemonic influence, but appropriation/social definition in domestic practice are not
findings.quote: 'Spatial structure itself is hegemonic,' but its appropriation and social definition in domestic practice are not (321:2).

findings.antecedent: Social structure of land use (home owners vs. apartment renters)
findings.consequent: Symbolic significance in everyday discourse about property
findings.quote: The classic study Everything in its Place: Social Order and Land Use in America (287) not only presents the social structure of land use, specifically the different perceptions of home owners and apartment renters in America, but also elaborates the symbolic significance of this system in the everyday discourse about renting and buying property in Houston and Philadelphia.

findings.consequent: Signifying system with symbolic meaning conveyed to dwellers and rural visitors
findings.quote: The City in Cultural Context (2) deals with 'city form as a signifying system that has symbolic meaning which is conveyed to city dwellers and rural visitors, and is absorbed by and acted upon by them' (2:284).

findings.consequent: Symbolic markers of class and social status in public and private buildings
findings.quote: Murray Edelman (94) is concerned with the legitimizing function of specific architectural features as symbolic markers of class and social status in public and private buildings.

findings.antecedent: Evolution of two Costa Rican plazas
findings.consequent: Contemporary meanings and user behavior (explained by historical, political economy, and symbolic analyses)
findings.quote: Low's study of the plaza (239) also integrates historical, political economy, and symbolic analyses of the evolution of two Costa Rican plazas in order to explain their contemporary meanings and user behavior.

findings.antecedent: History and occupancy of a handicapped-accessible housing cooperative
findings.consequent: Social construction of urban space
findings.quote: The ongoing study of Toronto cooperative housing by Margaret Rodman and Matt Cooper has generated a series of articles that explore the social construction of urban space through the history of the building and occupancy of a handicapped-accessible housing cooperative (327).

findings.consequent: Social use-value and aesthetic perspective
findings.quote: Mark Leone (230) brings together a social use-value and aesthetic perspective in his study of landscape architecture in the Chesapeake region of Maryland.

synthesis_conclusions: Social and cultural studies of human interactions with the built environment have grown significantly and are likely to receive more attention.
Social production theories are a promising new direction, placing built forms within the larger context of society's institutions and history.
The work of King, Castells, and Harvey has expanded political economy to include space as a dominant component and developed global systems theory for building analyses.
Bourdieu, Foucault, and Giddens have reintegrated spatial and temporal dimensions into social theory, providing a means to integrate built environment analysis with its role and meaning in society.
Buildings serve human needs, act as focal points for personal and social identities, and function as repositories of cultural information.
Architectural researchers' documentation techniques (e.g., axonometric drawing, photography) offer new ways for anthropologists to analyze the built environment.
Theories focusing on metaphor and designed architectural forms provide a fruitful starting point for collaboration between anthropologists and design professionals.
evidence_gaps: The processes by which people fulfill housing needs with built forms remain unclear.
Decision-making processes for building, remodeling, or moving are not well documented or understood in most societies studied by anthropologists.
The meaning of the built environment, as revealed through metaphorical connections and ritual practices, is an incompletely explored dimension.
Much research in social production has focused on theoretical development, often lacking empirical details at an abstract level.
Social production approaches (Bourdieu, Foucault, Giddens) have not yet integrated insights from symbolic and psychological studies.
The analysis and interpretation of building decisions cannot be understood in isolation from continuous social and economic institutional forces.
The interpretation of symbolic meaning cannot be divorced from social and economic forces or history.

paper_metadata.title: What are emotions? And how can they be measured?
paper_metadata.crossref_title: What are emotions? And how can they be measured?
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Defining “emotion” is a notorious problem. Without consensual conceptualization and operationalization of exactly what phenomenon is to be studied, progress in theory and research is difficult to achieve and fruitless debates are likely to proliferate. A particularly unfortunate example is William James’s asking the question “What is an emotion?” when he really meant “feeling”, a misnomer that started a debate which is still ongoing, more than a century later. This contribution attempts to sensitize researchers in the social and behavioral sciences to the importance of definitional issues and their consequences for distinguishing related but fundamentally different affective processes, states, and traits. Links between scientific and folk concepts of emotion are explored and ways to measure emotion and its components are discussed.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The spatial configuration of the built environment, rather than just individual elements, fundamentally shapes human movement patterns, social interaction, and the organization of social life.
The relational structure of space itself is a primary determinant of social function and human behavior within built environments.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper describes how the spatial configuration of built forms influences social interaction and collective endeavors.

steps.to_construct: Opportunities for social interaction and collective action
